prize_parts.citation: For realizing controllable strongly interacting quantum many-body systems with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, through the proposal and observation of the superfluid-Mott insulator transition and the development of single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy

statement.case_for: I keep B027 as my preferred single-part prize, but I now state the case more narrowly than in round 1. The decisive achievement is the observation of the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition in an optical lattice, which realised a textbook interacting lattice model, the Bose-Hubbard model, as a tunable system with parameters set by laser intensity, and which showed quantitatively the transition the theory predicted. Quantum gas microscopy is the second decisive step, because it made correlations readable site by site, which no solid-state Hubbard system allows. This is the combination I find scientifically compelling: a clean model, an analysable mechanism, and direct, independently reproduced experimental contact. Roughly two decades of reproduction by many groups, and tests of Hubbard physics (antiferromagnetic correlations, string patterns, thermalisation and localisation questions) against theory, show that the field is understood and not merely working. The attribution rule I propose is by role. Zoller supplied the theoretical programme for cold atoms as quantum simulators, Bloch's group made the transition experiment a quantitative, controlled study, and Greiner's group took the microscope to the Hubbard regime. After round 1 I did not move to B051 or B050, because the objections raised against B027 concern credit and platform status, which I can address, whereas the objections to B051 (overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes) and to B050 (the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap) concern what the achievement is. I do not claim B027 is the consensus choice. It is the one where, on my own judgement of mechanism and verification, the scientific case is strongest, and I am prepared to be outvoted on it.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and I have not removed it. Bloch, Greiner and Zoller is a three-way judgement over five credited names; Cirac and Dalibard have credible claims, and Jaksch, who wrote the 1998 Bose-Hubbard proposal with Zoller and Bruder, Cirac and Gardiner, is not on the list at all. A prize that names Zoller for the proposal while the transition experiment is credited to Bloch's group invites the objection that the proposal itself was shared. Much of the impact is as a platform, and the promise of solving problems that classical computers cannot is only partly delivered, so a sceptic can say that the lattice work is a superb instrument and not yet a discovery about nature. The overlap with the BEC (2001) and laser-cooling (1997) prizes and with trapped-ion and Rydberg simulators is real. Finally, B027 has the weakest support of my three named items: only I put it first, and Lindroth, who works in the neighbouring field, ranked it seventh.

responses.point: Lindroth asked me to argue a specific decisive experiment, noting that the Mott transition and microscope are impressive controls but that the platform payoff is partial and the choice of Bloch, Greiner and Zoller over Cirac and Dalibard seems arbitrary.
responses.response: The specific experiment I would name is the 2002 observation of the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition for bosons in a three-dimensional optical lattice. It is the result where nature was asked a sharp question, whether the interacting lattice model has a quantum phase transition at the predicted ratio of tunnelling to on-site interaction, and answered it, with the collapse and revival of the matter-wave phase as a clean signature. It was a surprise in the sense that matters to me: a strongly correlated state in a system that is almost free of disorder and decoherence. I accept your point about arbitrariness for the other two roles. My most defensible version is a rule by function: the person who made the programme (Zoller), the group that made the transition quantitative and later extended the platform (Bloch), and the group that delivered the first Hubbard-regime microscope (Greiner). If you consider that rule weaker than Cirac and Dalibard, I would like to hear the priority argument on the theory side, since you know this community better than I do. On overlap, the earlier prizes recognised how to cool and condense atoms. The Mott transition is a result about interactions, which neither of them addressed.

responses.point: Kroll supports B051 as the cleanest new measurement capability, with a compact two-name attribution and reproducibility through clock-to-clock comparisons between independent laboratories, and treats the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as a qualification and not a defeat.
responses.response: I take your reproducibility argument seriously, and it is the strongest feature of B051; the clock comparisons are exactly the kind of check I would want. Two points keep me from moving. First, the overlap objection is stronger for B051 than for B027, as you say yourself: the clock results are quantitative advances on an instrument class that the 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured, and the headline application, the redefinition of the second, is still prospective. Second, I would ask what physics has been learnt from lattice clocks that was not available from ion clocks at lower accuracy; the fundamental-physics results to date are limits. For B027 the corresponding question has an answer, because the Mott transition and the microscope gave direct access to correlations in a regime where theory is hard. I do not think this makes B051 a poor choice. I keep it as my second alternative, and if the committee goes there I would support Katori and Ye, with the citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice, as Lindroth suggests, and not general accuracy.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B050 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a verified, reproduced discovery of a new state of electronic matter that nature made available once theory showed where to look, with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap and the 2016 topology prize as the main qualifications.
responses.response: I agree that B050 is the strongest single discovery on the table in the sense you describe, and it stays as my first alternative. The Z2 classification is a clean piece of theory with an experiment that tested it, and I do not regard it as premature. My concern is about what the citation can honestly say. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the host and Molenkamp tested that proposal, so excluding them in a trio makes the prize read as if Kane and Mele predicted the material, which they did not. The 2016 prize recognised topological phases and phase transitions, and a second prize for a theme closely related to it needs a clear statement of what is new, namely the time-reversal-invariant Z2 case and its observation. You asked, implicitly, whether the lattice case is only indirect. I would say that B027 is also open on credit, so I do not claim an advantage there. The difference I would offer is that for B050 the omitted people are essential to the experiment's logic, whereas for B027 the omitted people are alternative holders of a role that others also fill. That is a judgement, and I would accept an outside report on both.

uncertainties: Which three of Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Cirac and Dalibard (with Jaksch unlisted) is the defensible set; I rely on memory for the priority history of the 1998 Bose-Hubbard proposal, the 2002 transition experiment and the microscopy work, and I would welcome an outside expert report on this before the final ballot.

Whether the committee regards ultracold-atom lattices as distinct enough from the BEC and laser-cooling prizes, and whether a platform prize meets the committee's standard of a discovery or invention.
Whether the quantum simulation payoff, which is partly delivered, is sufficient maturity, or whether the committee should wait for clearer results on problems that are out of reach classically.

Whether B050 or B051 would hold up better against the priority and novelty objections than I currently estimate; I cannot settle the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question or the Lemonde priority question from memory.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I have no collaboration with any of the names credited in B027, B050 or B051. I note a general institutional proximity to Johansson and Olsson in the Gothenburg physics environment, which is relevant only to B038 or B033, and Johansson has already disclosed that he would recuse on B038. I would not need to recuse on any shortlisted candidate. My field (turbulent aerosols, random-matrix theory, statistical physics) is adjacent to many-body physics but I have no stake in the outcome.
